scenarios.scenarioText: Zenova Pharmaceuticals Ltd. (ZPL), a company listed on BSE and NSE with a market capitalisation of Rs. 12,400 crore and 1,85,000 shareholders, received USFDA approval for its breakthrough cancer drug 'Oncozil' on March 3, 2026. The approval was communicated to the company's Managing Director, Dr. Rakesh Sinha, at 9:15 AM IST, prior to market opening. However, the company did not make the announcement to the stock exchanges until 3:45 PM — nearly 30 minutes before market close. SEBI's surveillance division detected unusual trading activity between 10:00 AM and 3:30 PM on March 3, 2026: over 2.8 lakh shares were purchased through 47 unique trading accounts linked to six brokers, resulting in a price surge of 14.2% before the public announcement. SEBI received formal complaints from the Investor Protection Association (IPA) and from two minority shareholders — Mr. Arvind Kothari (holding 0.8% equity) and Ms. Shalini Desai (holding 0.003% equity). SEBI's Whole Time Member (WTM), Ms. Kavita Nair, passed an ex parte ad interim order on March 10, 2026, directing ZPL's promoter group (holding 48.6% equity), Dr. Rakesh Sinha personally, the company secretary Mr. Deepak Joshi, and the CFO Ms. Pallavi Reddy to not buy, sell, or deal in securities of ZPL until further orders. The order also froze the demat accounts of 12 individuals identified as 'connected persons.' SEBI's investigation division simultaneously appointed Mr. K. Ramachandran, a Senior General Manager, as the Investigating Authority (IA) under the relevant provisions. The IA summoned Dr. Sinha for examination on oath on March 18, 2026, and also issued notices to all six brokers directing them to furnish trading data, communication records, and client KYC details within 15 days. Broker Alpha Securities Ltd. (registered as a stockbroker under SEBI) refused to provide communication records, citing client confidentiality under its internal privacy policy. Another entity, Omega Research Advisory (not registered with SEBI but providing stock tips on social media with 4.2 lakh followers), was also found to have issued a 'strong buy' recommendation on ZPL at 10:30 AM on March 3, 2026, before the public announcement. SEBI's Legal Affairs division is now evaluating whether to initiate disgorgement proceedings, seek a consent order, or recommend criminal prosecution referral.

questions.question: Regarding the ex parte ad interim order passed by WTM Ms. Kavita Nair on March 10, 2026, freezing dealings and demat accounts, under which provision of the SEBI Act, 1992 does SEBI derive this power, and which of the following statements about this power is CORRECT?

options.A: Under Section 11C, SEBI can pass such orders during the course of an investigation, and the order must be confirmed by the SEBI Board within 30 days failing which it lapses automatically
options.B: Under Section 11B, SEBI can issue directions in the interest of investors or the securities market, including interim orders, and such directions can include prohibiting persons from buying, selling, or dealing in securities
options.C: Under Section 11(4), SEBI can pass such orders only after completing a full investigation under Section 11C and recording a finding of violation, and the power cannot be exercised on an ex parte basis
options.D: Under Section 12, SEBI can freeze demat accounts of registered intermediaries only, and since Dr. Sinha and the promoter group are not registered intermediaries, the freezing of their accounts is ultra vires SEBI's powers

questions.explanation: Under Section 11B of the SEBI Act, 1992, SEBI has the power to issue directions in the interest of investors or the securities market. This power is extremely broad and includes the ability to issue interim/ex parte orders prohibiting persons from dealing in securities, freezing demat accounts, and directing disgorgement. The WTM exercises this power as a delegate of the SEBI Board. Option A is the most tempting trap — it attributes the power to Section 11C, which deals specifically with investigation (appointing IA, summoning persons, etc.), NOT with issuing directions or interim orders. Section 11C empowers SEBI to investigate, while Section 11B empowers SEBI to issue directions — these are distinct powers. Option C incorrectly states that a full investigation must be completed before directions can be issued; the whole point of interim orders is that they are passed BEFORE the investigation concludes. Option D wrongly limits SEBI's direction power to registered intermediaries only — Section 11B directions can be issued against any person in the securities market. The scenario fact that the order was 'ex parte ad interim' confirms it was passed under Section 11B's direction-making power without prior hearing.

questions.question: SEBI appointed Mr. K. Ramachandran, a Senior General Manager, as the Investigating Authority (IA) under Section 11C. The IA summoned Dr. Sinha for examination on oath. Which of the following statements about the IA's powers under Section 11C is INCORRECT?

options.A: The IA can require any person, including Dr. Sinha, to produce books, registers, documents, and records, and can retain them for a period not exceeding 30 days from the date of production
options.B: The IA has the power to examine on oath any person associated with the securities market, and any statement made by Dr. Sinha during such examination can be used in evidence against him in subsequent proceedings
options.C: The IA can require any intermediary or person associated with the securities market to furnish information or produce records, and every such person is bound to comply with the IA's requisition
options.D: The IA appointed under Section 11C exercises powers akin to those of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, including the power to summon and enforce attendance of witnesses and to order discovery and production of documents

questions.explanation: The INCORRECT statement is Option A. Under Section 11C of the SEBI Act, the Investigating Authority does NOT have a specific limitation of '30 days' for retention of books and documents. This 30-day retention period is a fabrication designed to trap students who confuse it with other statutory retention periods (such as the 180-day retention under Section 207 of the Companies Act for inspectors). The IA under Section 11C can retain documents as long as necessary for the investigation. Option B is correct — Section 11C(8) provides that statements made during examination on oath are admissible in evidence. Option C is correct — Section 11C(3) imposes a duty on every person to produce documents when required by the IA, making Broker Alpha Securities' refusal a violation. Option D is correct — Section 11C(9) confers civil court powers on the IA. The scenario's mention of Mr. Ramachandran being a 'Senior General Manager' is a red herring — the Act does not prescribe a minimum rank for the IA (unlike the Adjudicating Officer under Section 15I which requires minimum Division Chief rank).

questions.question: Broker Alpha Securities Ltd. refused to provide communication records citing its internal privacy policy. Simultaneously, Omega Research Advisory (unregistered with SEBI) issued stock recommendations on social media. Considering the facts in the scenario, which of the following correctly states the legal position regarding BOTH entities?

options.A: Alpha Securities' refusal is legally valid because client confidentiality is a statutory obligation of registered stockbrokers under SEBI regulations, which overrides the IA's investigatory power; Omega Research Advisory cannot be proceeded against since it is not registered with SEBI and falls outside SEBI's jurisdiction
options.B: Alpha Securities is bound to comply with the IA's requisition under Section 11C and its refusal constitutes a violation; however, Omega Research Advisory, being unregistered, can only be proceeded against under criminal law by police authorities and not by SEBI
options.C: Alpha Securities is bound to comply under Section 11C regardless of its internal privacy policy, and its refusal can attract penalty under Section 15A; Omega Research Advisory, despite being unregistered, can be proceeded against by SEBI under Section 11B for operating as an unregistered investment adviser and under Section 12 for the registration violation
options.D: Alpha Securities can refuse communication records but must provide trading data and KYC details; Omega Research Advisory is beyond SEBI's regulatory reach since social media activity does not constitute 'securities market' activity under the SEBI Act

questions.explanation: Option C correctly states the position on both entities. For Alpha Securities: Under Section 11C(3)-(4), every intermediary and person associated with the securities market is BOUND to produce documents and records when required by the Investigating Authority. No internal privacy policy can override this statutory obligation. The refusal to furnish information attracts penalty under Section 15A (up to Rs. 1 lakh per day, maximum Rs. 1 crore). For Omega Research Advisory: Despite being unregistered, SEBI's jurisdiction extends to any person associated with the securities market. Under Section 12, providing investment advice without registration is itself a violation. Under Section 11B, SEBI can issue directions against any person in the interest of investors. Option A is the 'obvious but wrong' answer — client confidentiality does NOT override statutory investigation powers. Option B correctly identifies Alpha's obligation but wrongly states that unregistered entities can only be dealt with by police — SEBI has jurisdiction over unregistered entities operating in the securities market. Option D creates a false distinction between types of records and wrongly excludes social media activity from SEBI's jurisdiction. The scenario fact that Omega has 4.2 lakh followers providing stock tips makes it clearly within SEBI's regulatory purview.

questions.question: SEBI's Legal Affairs division is evaluating whether to initiate disgorgement proceedings, seek a consent order, or recommend criminal prosecution. Regarding the relationship between disgorgement under Section 11B and criminal prosecution under Section 24, which of the following statements is CORRECT in the context of the ZPL investigation?

options.A: SEBI must choose between disgorgement and criminal prosecution — it cannot pursue both simultaneously against the same person for the same set of facts, as this would violate the principle of double jeopardy under Article 20(2) of the Constitution
options.B: Disgorgement under Section 11B is a civil remedy that operates independently of criminal prosecution under Section 24; SEBI can simultaneously order disgorgement of ill-gotten gains AND recommend criminal prosecution, since one is remedial and the other is punitive
options.C: Criminal prosecution under Section 24 can only be initiated after the disgorgement proceedings under Section 11B are concluded and the disgorged amount has been recovered, as prosecution is a last resort when civil remedies fail
options.D: Disgorgement under Section 11B can only be ordered by the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) on appeal from SEBI's order, and SEBI itself does not have the power to directly order disgorgement in the first instance

questions.explanation: Option B is correct. Disgorgement under Section 11B is a civil/remedial measure — SEBI orders the person to 'disgorge' (surrender) the profits made or losses avoided through the violation. Criminal prosecution under Section 24 is a separate punitive track where the person faces imprisonment (up to 10 years) and/or fine (up to Rs. 25 crore). These are independent remedies that can be pursued simultaneously. Option A is the most common trap — students confuse civil disgorgement with criminal punishment and invoke double jeopardy. However, double jeopardy applies only to criminal proceedings, not to civil-criminal parallel proceedings. Disgorgement is not a 'punishment' but a restitution/remedial measure. Option C incorrectly creates a sequential requirement — there is no provision requiring civil remedies to be exhausted before criminal prosecution. Option D wrongly attributes disgorgement power to SAT instead of SEBI — Section 11B explicitly empowers SEBI (not SAT) to order disgorgement. The scenario mentions SEBI evaluating all three options, and the legal position is that disgorgement and criminal prosecution can run in parallel.

questions.question: Considering that SEBI's functions under Section 11 include protecting investor interests and regulating the securities market, and given the specific facts of the ZPL case — including the 14.2% price surge, 47 unique trading accounts across six brokers, and the 5.5-hour delay in announcing the USFDA approval — which of the following BEST describes the scope of SEBI's regulatory authority in this scenario?

options.A: SEBI can regulate and investigate the trading activity of the 47 accounts and the six brokers, but it cannot take action against ZPL's board for the delayed disclosure because the timing of corporate announcements falls exclusively under the stock exchange's listing agreement jurisdiction, not SEBI's
options.B: SEBI's authority is limited to regulating registered intermediaries (the six brokers) and cannot extend to the 12 'connected persons' whose demat accounts were frozen, because natural persons who are not registered intermediaries fall outside the scope of Section 11
options.C: SEBI has comprehensive authority under Section 11 to take measures for investor protection and market regulation, which encompasses investigating the suspicious trading, taking action against the brokers, the connected persons, ZPL's board for delayed disclosure, and Omega Research Advisory for unregistered advisory activity
options.D: SEBI's jurisdiction in this case is limited because the USFDA approval is a foreign regulatory action, and SEBI can only regulate events originating from Indian regulatory decisions; the appropriate authority for investigating insider trading based on foreign regulatory approvals is the Ministry of Corporate Affairs

questions.explanation: Option C is correct. Section 11(1) of the SEBI Act vests SEBI with the duty to protect investor interests and regulate the securities market. Section 11(2) enumerates specific measures SEBI can take, including regulating insider trading, prohibiting fraudulent trade practices, and taking measures for investor protection. This is a comprehensive authority that covers ALL aspects of the scenario: the suspicious trading by 47 accounts (potential insider trading), the six brokers (registered intermediaries), the connected persons (Section 11B directions), ZPL's board for delayed disclosure of material information (LODR compliance), and Omega Research Advisory for unregistered investment advisory activity (Section 12). Option A is the 'close but not quite' trap — while stock exchanges do administer listing agreements, SEBI has overriding regulatory authority over listed companies and their disclosure obligations through LODR regulations framed under the SEBI Act. Option B wrongly limits SEBI's authority to registered intermediaries — Section 11B allows directions against ANY person in the securities market. Option D is absurd on closer reading but may trap students who overthink jurisdictional boundaries — SEBI's jurisdiction is based on where the trading occurs (Indian securities market), not where the underlying event originates. The 5.5-hour delay mentioned in the scenario is a key fact establishing the delayed disclosure violation.

scenarios.scenarioText: Mr. Harish Khurana, a SEBI-registered stockbroker operating through his firm 'Khurana Capital Services' (KCS), was involved in multiple violations during the period January 2025 to December 2025. First, SEBI issued a notice dated February 5, 2025, directing KCS to furnish details of all proprietary trades executed between January 1, 2025, and January 31, 2025, within 15 days. KCS did not furnish the information. SEBI issued a second notice on March 10, 2025, granting a further 10 days. KCS again failed to comply. The total period of non-compliance (from the expiry of the first deadline i.e., February 20, 2025) until the date when KCS finally furnished partial information (June 15, 2025) was 115 days. Second, an investigation revealed that Mr. Khurana personally traded in the shares of Globex Industries Ltd. between April 5 and April 12, 2025, while in possession of unpublished price-sensitive information (UPSI) regarding Globex's upcoming merger with NovaTech Corp. Mr. Khurana purchased 50,000 shares at an average price of Rs. 340 per share and sold them on April 28, 2025, at Rs. 520 per share after the merger was publicly announced on April 25, 2025. His total profit from these trades was Rs. 90,00,000 (Rs. 90 lakh). Third, during the same period, KCS executed a series of synchronised trades in the shares of Pinnacle Infra Ltd. through two client accounts — Mr. Rajiv Malhotra and Ms. Anita Bhatia — creating an artificial appearance of trading activity and inflating the share price by 23% over three weeks. The artificial volume generated was approximately Rs. 45 crore. After SEBI's investigation, the Adjudicating Officer quantified the unlawful gain from the synchronised trading at Rs. 7.8 crore. SEBI's Adjudicating Officer, Mr. V. Suresh, who holds the rank of Deputy General Manager in SEBI's enforcement division, was assigned to adjudicate all three violations. Mr. Khurana's legal counsel has raised preliminary objections regarding the computation of penalties and the competence of the Adjudicating Officer.

questions.question: Regarding the penalty for KCS's failure to furnish information for 115 days (from February 20, 2025, to June 15, 2025), which of the following correctly computes the MAXIMUM penalty imposable under Section 15A of the SEBI Act?

options.A: Rs. 1,15,00,000 (Rs. 1.15 crore), computed at Rs. 1 lakh per day for 115 days, since Section 15A prescribes a penalty of Rs. 1 lakh for each day of default with no upper ceiling
options.B: Rs. 1,00,00,000 (Rs. 1 crore), because although the per-day computation yields Rs. 1.15 crore (Rs. 1 lakh x 115 days), Section 15A caps the maximum penalty at Rs. 1 crore
options.C: Rs. 57,50,000 (Rs. 57.5 lakh), computed at Rs. 50,000 per day for 115 days, as the per-day penalty under Section 15A is Rs. 50,000, not Rs. 1 lakh
options.D: Rs. 25,00,000 (Rs. 25 lakh), because the penalty under Section 15A is a fixed lump sum of Rs. 25 lakh for failure to furnish information, regardless of the number of days of default

questions.explanation: Under Section 15A of the SEBI Act, the penalty for failure to furnish information, documents, or return as required is up to Rs. 1 lakh for each day during which such failure continues, subject to a maximum of Rs. 1 crore. In this case, the per-day computation is Rs. 1 lakh x 115 days = Rs. 1,15,00,000 (Rs. 1.15 crore). However, since Section 15A imposes a CAP of Rs. 1 crore, the maximum penalty cannot exceed Rs. 1,00,00,000 (Rs. 1 crore). Option A is the most tempting trap — it correctly computes the per-day amount but IGNORES the Rs. 1 crore statutory cap, which is the critical detail students must know. The scenario deliberately uses 115 days (exceeding 100 days) to ensure the per-day computation exceeds the cap, forcing students to apply the ceiling. Option C uses a wrong per-day figure of Rs. 50,000 (a fabricated number). Option D invents a lump sum penalty. The key scenario fact is the 115-day period, which when multiplied by Rs. 1 lakh/day = Rs. 1.15 crore, triggering the Rs. 1 crore cap.

questions.question: Mr. Khurana made a profit of Rs. 90 lakh from insider trading in Globex Industries shares. Under Section 15G of the SEBI Act, what is the MAXIMUM penalty that can be imposed on Mr. Khurana for this insider trading violation?

options.A: Rs. 25 crore, because Section 15G prescribes a maximum penalty of Rs. 25 crore for insider trading violations, and since Rs. 90 lakh is less than Rs. 25 crore, the penalty is capped at Rs. 25 crore
options.B: Rs. 2,70,00,000 (Rs. 2.70 crore), computed as three times the profit made (3 x Rs. 90 lakh), because Section 15G prescribes the penalty as three times the amount of profits made out of insider trading
options.C: Rs. 25 crore, because Section 15G prescribes a penalty which shall not be less than Rs. 10 lakh but which may extend to Rs. 25 crore or three times the amount of profits made, whichever is HIGHER, and since Rs. 25 crore is higher than 3 x Rs. 90 lakh (Rs. 2.70 crore), the maximum penalty is Rs. 25 crore
options.D: Rs. 2,70,00,000 (Rs. 2.70 crore), because Section 15G prescribes a penalty of Rs. 25 crore or three times the profit, whichever is LOWER, and since 3 x Rs. 90 lakh = Rs. 2.70 crore is lower than Rs. 25 crore, the penalty is Rs. 2.70 crore

questions.explanation: Under Section 15G of the SEBI Act, the penalty for insider trading is not less than Rs. 10 lakh but may extend to Rs. 25 crore or three times the amount of profits made out of insider trading, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER. This is the most critical trap in SEBI penalty provisions. In this case: 3 x Rs. 90 lakh = Rs. 2.70 crore. Comparing Rs. 25 crore vs Rs. 2.70 crore — Rs. 25 crore is higher. Therefore, the maximum penalty is Rs. 25 crore. Option A states the correct answer (Rs. 25 crore) but with incomplete reasoning — it does not mention the 3x computation, making it an incomplete understanding. Option C provides the complete and correct reasoning. Option B is the trap for students who know about the '3x profit' rule but forget the 'Rs. 25 crore OR 3x, whichever is HIGHER' formulation. Option D reverses the rule to 'whichever is LOWER' — a classic reversal trap. The scenario deliberately uses a profit figure (Rs. 90 lakh) where 3x (Rs. 2.70 crore) is LESS than Rs. 25 crore, forcing students to apply the 'whichever is higher' rule correctly.

questions.question: For the synchronised trading (fraudulent/unfair trade practice) in Pinnacle Infra shares that generated an unlawful gain of Rs. 7.8 crore, what is the MAXIMUM penalty imposable under Section 15HA of the SEBI Act, and how does it compare with the insider trading penalty under Section 15G?

options.A: Under Section 15HA, the maximum penalty is Rs. 25 crore or 3x profit (whichever is higher); since 3 x Rs. 7.8 crore = Rs. 23.4 crore, which is LESS than Rs. 25 crore, the maximum is Rs. 25 crore — this is the SAME formula as Section 15G, and both penalties can be imposed cumulatively for separate violations
options.B: Under Section 15HA, the maximum penalty is Rs. 25 crore (fixed cap, no 3x computation), which is DIFFERENT from Section 15G where the 3x computation applies; thus the Sec 15HA penalty for Pinnacle Infra is Rs. 25 crore while Sec 15G penalty for Globex is also Rs. 25 crore, but they are computed differently
options.C: Under Section 15HA, the maximum penalty is Rs. 1 crore (similar to Section 15HB for 'other contraventions'), and since the unlawful gain is Rs. 7.8 crore which exceeds Rs. 1 crore, SEBI must pursue criminal prosecution under Section 24 instead of adjudication
options.D: Under Section 15HA, the maximum penalty is 3x profit only (no Rs. 25 crore alternative), yielding Rs. 23.4 crore; this is different from Section 15G which has the higher Rs. 25 crore cap, making the Sec 15G penalty higher despite the lower profit in Globex trades

questions.explanation: Option A is correct. Section 15HA (fraudulent and unfair trade practices) prescribes the SAME penalty formula as Section 15G (insider trading): not less than Rs. 10 lakh but which may extend to Rs. 25 crore or three times the amount of profits made, whichever is HIGHER. For Pinnacle Infra: 3 x Rs. 7.8 crore = Rs. 23.4 crore. Since Rs. 25 crore > Rs. 23.4 crore, the maximum penalty is Rs. 25 crore. Crucially, since the insider trading (Globex) and the fraudulent trade practice (Pinnacle Infra) are SEPARATE violations, the penalties can be imposed cumulatively — up to Rs. 25 crore for each violation. Option B is the 'close but not quite' trap — it incorrectly claims that Section 15HA does not have the 3x computation, when in fact it mirrors Section 15G exactly. Option C deliberately confuses Section 15HA with Section 15HB (which has a Rs. 1 crore cap for 'other contraventions'). Option D inverts the formula by removing the Rs. 25 crore alternative. The key scenario facts are the two different profit figures (Rs. 90 lakh for Globex insider trading vs Rs. 7.8 crore for Pinnacle Infra synchronised trading), requiring separate penalty computations under different sections.

questions.question: Mr. Khurana's legal counsel has raised a preliminary objection regarding the competence of Mr. V. Suresh, the Adjudicating Officer, who holds the rank of Deputy General Manager. Under Section 15I of the SEBI Act, which of the following statements CORRECTLY evaluates this objection?

options.A: The objection is without merit because Section 15I does not prescribe any minimum rank for the Adjudicating Officer; SEBI can appoint any of its officers as Adjudicating Officer
options.B: The objection has merit because Section 15I requires the Adjudicating Officer to be not below the rank of a Division Chief, and a Deputy General Manager ranks below a Division Chief in SEBI's hierarchy
options.C: The objection is without merit because Section 15I requires the Adjudicating Officer to be not below the rank of a Deputy General Manager, and Mr. Suresh meets this requirement exactly
options.D: The objection has merit because only a Whole Time Member of SEBI can act as an Adjudicating Officer for violations involving penalties exceeding Rs. 10 crore, and the combined penalties here could exceed Rs. 10 crore

questions.explanation: Under Section 15I of the SEBI Act, the Adjudicating Officer must be an officer of SEBI not below the rank of a Division Chief. A Deputy General Manager (DGM) ranks BELOW a Division Chief in SEBI's organisational hierarchy (the hierarchy typically runs: DGM → General Manager → Chief General Manager → Executive Director, with Division Chief being equivalent to or above General Manager level). Since Mr. V. Suresh holds the rank of Deputy General Manager, he does NOT meet the minimum rank requirement, and Mr. Khurana's preliminary objection is well-founded. Option A is wrong because Section 15I DOES prescribe a minimum rank. Option C is a cleverly designed trap — it changes the minimum rank from 'Division Chief' to 'Deputy General Manager,' which sounds plausible but is factually incorrect. Option D fabricates a threshold-based competence rule for WTMs that does not exist. The scenario deliberately mentions Mr. Suresh's exact rank to test whether students know the minimum rank requirement under Section 15I. Any order passed by an incompetent Adjudicating Officer would be void ab initio.

questions.question: Assuming that a competent Adjudicating Officer is appointed and all three penalties are imposed at their maximum permissible levels, which of the following correctly represents the TOTAL maximum penalty exposure for Mr. Khurana/KCS across all three violations?

options.A: Rs. 51 crore: Section 15A (Rs. 1 crore) + Section 15G (Rs. 25 crore) + Section 15HA (Rs. 25 crore), since penalties for separate violations are cumulative and each section has its own independent cap
options.B: Rs. 25 crore: Because where multiple violations are adjudicated simultaneously, the overall penalty is limited to the highest single penalty applicable among all violations, which is Rs. 25 crore under either Section 15G or 15HA
options.C: Rs. 26 crore: Section 15A (Rs. 1 crore) + Section 15G (Rs. 25 crore) only, because the fraudulent trade practice penalty under Section 15HA merges into the insider trading penalty under Section 15G when both arise from securities market manipulation
options.D: Rs. 50.70 crore: Section 15A (Rs. 1.15 crore without cap) + Section 15G (Rs. 25 crore) + Section 15HA (3 x Rs. 7.8 crore = Rs. 23.4 crore, since for Sec 15HA the 3x profit always applies), plus Rs. 1.15 crore under Section 15HB for the registration-related violation

questions.explanation: Option A correctly states that the maximum penalty exposure is Rs. 51 crore. Each violation is adjudicated under its own section, and penalties under different sections are cumulative — there is no provision in the SEBI Act that limits the aggregate penalty when multiple violations are established. Section 15A: maximum Rs. 1 crore (capped, as computed in Q6). Section 15G (insider trading in Globex): maximum Rs. 25 crore (being higher of Rs. 25 crore or 3 x Rs. 90 lakh = Rs. 2.70 crore). Section 15HA (fraudulent practices in Pinnacle Infra): maximum Rs. 25 crore (being higher of Rs. 25 crore or 3 x Rs. 7.8 crore = Rs. 23.4 crore). Total = Rs. 1 crore + Rs. 25 crore + Rs. 25 crore = Rs. 51 crore. Option B is the trap for students who assume there is an overall cap or merger of penalties. Option C fabricates a merger doctrine between Sec 15G and 15HA. Option D contains multiple errors: it ignores the Rs. 1 crore cap on Sec 15A (using Rs. 1.15 crore), applies only 3x for Sec 15HA (ignoring the 'whichever is higher' rule), and adds a non-existent Sec 15HB violation. This question tests cumulative application of penalties — each scenario violation maps to a different penalty section.

scenarios.scenarioText: Apex Wealth Advisors Pvt. Ltd. (AWA) was registered with SEBI as an Investment Adviser (IA) under the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013. AWA's principal officer, Mr. Nitin Agarwal, held a NISM certification and had 12 years of experience in financial advisory. In November 2025, SEBI received complaints from 14 clients alleging that AWA had been: (a) guaranteeing minimum 18% annual returns on equity investments, (b) managing client funds directly by operating their trading accounts through power of attorney, and (c) charging fees linked to portfolio profits (i.e., performance-based fees) without proper disclosure. Meanwhile, Mr. Agarwal's associate, Ms. Prerna Saxena, who did not hold any SEBI registration, was independently providing portfolio management services to high-net-worth clients (minimum ticket size Rs. 25 lakh) through her firm 'WealthCraft Solutions.' She advertised her services as 'SEBI-approved portfolio management' on her website and LinkedIn profile. SEBI's intermediary supervision department initiated an inspection of AWA's operations and simultaneously issued a show-cause notice to Ms. Saxena's firm. The inspection revealed that AWA had also been acting as a de facto portfolio manager — pooling client funds, making investment decisions without individual client mandates, and charging a 20% profit-sharing fee. AWA's total client base was 340 individuals with aggregate assets under advice of Rs. 180 crore. SEBI issued an interim order under Section 11B on January 5, 2026, suspending AWA's IA registration and restraining Mr. Agarwal from accessing the securities market. AWA challenged this order, arguing that (i) suspension requires a prior show-cause notice and opportunity of hearing, (ii) SEBI should have proceeded under the IA Regulations rather than under the SEBI Act directly, and (iii) the activities described fall within the legitimate scope of investment advisory services. SEBI's enforcement division is now considering whether to cancel AWA's registration permanently under Section 12, impose monetary penalties through adjudication, and/or refer the matter for criminal prosecution under Section 24. The compliance officer of National Stock Exchange (NSE) has also flagged that 28 of AWA's client accounts showed unusual trading patterns consistent with front-running.

questions.question: Regarding AWA's argument that SEBI's interim suspension order under Section 11B is invalid because it was passed without prior show-cause notice and opportunity of hearing, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: AWA's argument is valid because Section 11B mandates that no direction shall be issued without giving the person concerned a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and an ex parte interim order violates this mandatory requirement
options.B: AWA's argument is partially valid — while SEBI can pass interim orders under Section 11B without prior hearing, such orders must be confirmed by the Securities Appellate Tribunal within 15 days, failing which they lapse automatically
options.C: AWA's argument is not valid because SEBI can pass ex parte interim orders under Section 11B in the interest of investors or the securities market, provided that a post-decisional hearing is granted within a reasonable time and the interim order is confirmed or revoked after such hearing
options.D: AWA's argument is valid because under Section 12, only the registration-granting authority (which is the SEBI Board, not the WTM) can suspend or cancel registration, and the WTM's interim direction under Section 11B cannot effectively achieve what only the SEBI Board can do under Section 12

questions.explanation: Option C is correct. SEBI has the power to pass ex parte interim orders under Section 11B in urgent situations where investor interests or market integrity are at stake. The Supreme Court has upheld SEBI's power to pass interim orders without prior hearing, subject to the condition that a post-decisional hearing must be granted within a reasonable time. The interim order remains in force until confirmed or revoked after such hearing. AWA's argument that prior hearing is mandatory for ALL Section 11B directions is incorrect. Option A is the strongest trap — while Section 11B does contain a requirement for opportunity of hearing, this has been interpreted to include post-decisional hearing for interim orders. The word 'reasonable opportunity' does not mean 'prior opportunity' in every case. Option B fabricates a 15-day SAT confirmation requirement that does not exist in the SEBI Act — there is no automatic lapse provision. Option D raises a superficially appealing jurisdictional argument but is wrong because Section 11B gives independent direction-making power that operates alongside (not subordinate to) Section 12. The scenario fact that the order was passed as an 'interim order' is crucial — interim orders by their nature require urgency and can be ex parte.

questions.question: Ms. Prerna Saxena's firm WealthCraft Solutions provides portfolio management services without SEBI registration and advertises itself as 'SEBI-approved.' Regarding SEBI's jurisdiction over WealthCraft Solutions, which of the following is INCORRECT?

options.A: SEBI can issue directions under Section 11B restraining WealthCraft Solutions from operating in the securities market, even though WealthCraft is not registered with SEBI, because Section 11B directions can be issued against any person in the interest of investors
options.B: Operating as a portfolio manager without registration under Section 12 is a violation of the SEBI Act, and WealthCraft Solutions can be proceeded against both under Section 11B (directions) and through adjudication proceedings for the penalty under Section 15HB
options.C: SEBI can initiate criminal prosecution under Section 24 against Ms. Saxena for operating without registration, as contravention of Section 12 read with SEBI regulations is a prosecutable offence carrying imprisonment up to 10 years or fine up to Rs. 25 crore or both
options.D: SEBI must first issue a registration to WealthCraft Solutions and then suspend or cancel it before taking any enforcement action, because SEBI's regulatory powers under Sections 11B and 12 only apply to registered intermediaries and registered entities

questions.explanation: Option D is the INCORRECT statement (and therefore the correct answer to this 'which is INCORRECT' question). SEBI does NOT need to first register an entity before it can take enforcement action against it. SEBI's regulatory powers under Section 11B extend to ANY person in the securities market, whether registered or not. The very violation being alleged — operating without registration — would be defeated if SEBI had to first register the entity. This is a logical absurdity. Options A, B, and C are all CORRECT statements: (A) Section 11B empowers SEBI to issue directions against any person; (B) Operating without registration violates Section 12, attractable to Section 15HB penalty (up to Rs. 1 crore); (C) Section 24 criminal prosecution can be initiated for contravention of the SEBI Act. Option D is designed to trap students who incorrectly believe SEBI's enforcement jurisdiction is limited to registered entities. The scenario fact that WealthCraft advertises itself as 'SEBI-approved' despite having no registration adds a misrepresentation element, strengthening SEBI's case further.

questions.question: AWA was found to be operating as a de facto portfolio manager despite holding only an Investment Adviser registration. The penalty for this 'other contravention' (operating beyond the scope of registration) would fall under which section, and what is the maximum penalty?

options.A: Section 15G, with a maximum penalty of Rs. 25 crore or 3x profits, whichever is higher, because operating beyond scope of registration while in possession of client information constitutes insider trading
options.B: Section 15HA, with a maximum penalty of Rs. 25 crore or 3x profits, whichever is higher, because operating as a portfolio manager under the guise of investment advisory constitutes a 'fraudulent and unfair trade practice'
options.C: Section 15HB, with a maximum penalty of Rs. 1 crore, because operating beyond the scope of one's registration is a contravention of the SEBI Act and regulations for which no specific penalty is provided under Sections 15A to 15HA
options.D: Section 15A, with a maximum penalty of Rs. 1 crore (Rs. 1 lakh per day), because AWA's failure to confine itself to its registered activity constitutes a continuing failure to comply with SEBI's regulatory requirements

questions.explanation: Option C is correct. Section 15HB is the residual/catch-all penalty provision that applies to contraventions of the SEBI Act or regulations for which no SPECIFIC penalty is provided elsewhere in Chapter VIA. Operating beyond the scope of one's registration (acting as a portfolio manager with only an IA licence) is a contravention of SEBI regulations, but it does not specifically fall under insider trading (15G), non-disclosure under takeover (15H), fraudulent trade practices (15HA), or failure to furnish information (15A). The maximum penalty under Section 15HB is Rs. 1 crore. Option A is a trap — operating beyond scope has nothing to do with insider trading under Section 15G, which requires trading while in possession of UPSI. Option B is a tempting distractor — while AWA's conduct could arguably involve 'unfair' practices, Section 15HA specifically targets 'fraudulent and unfair trade practices' as defined in the SEBI (PFUTP) Regulations, not scope-of-registration violations. Option D misapplies Section 15A, which deals with failure to furnish information/returns, not failure to confine to registered activity. The key distinction is between specific penalty sections (15A-15HA) and the residual section (15HB).

questions.question: SEBI is considering whether to cancel AWA's registration permanently under Section 12. Regarding SEBI's power to suspend or cancel the registration of an intermediary, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: SEBI can suspend registration for a maximum period of 6 months, after which it must either restore the registration or cancel it; suspension cannot be extended beyond 6 months under any circumstances
options.B: SEBI can suspend or cancel registration only through an order of the SEBI Board at a full Board meeting; a Whole Time Member acting alone cannot pass a final cancellation order under Section 12
options.C: SEBI can suspend or cancel the registration of an intermediary after holding an inquiry, and such suspension or cancellation can be ordered by SEBI in the prescribed manner, subject to the intermediary's right to appeal to SAT under Section 15T
options.D: SEBI can only suspend registration (temporary measure) but cannot cancel registration permanently; permanent cancellation requires an order from the Securities Appellate Tribunal under Section 15Z

questions.explanation: Option C is correct. Under Section 12(3)/(4) of the SEBI Act, SEBI has the power to suspend or cancel the registration of any intermediary in the prescribed manner after conducting an inquiry. The intermediary has the right to appeal such suspension/cancellation order to the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) under Section 15T. Option A fabricates a 6-month maximum suspension period — no such limitation exists in the SEBI Act. The duration of suspension is at SEBI's discretion. Option B incorrectly claims that only the SEBI Board (not a WTM) can cancel registration — the SEBI Act and regulations permit delegation to WTMs for enforcement actions. Option D wrongly states that permanent cancellation can only be ordered by SAT — SAT is an appellate body that reviews SEBI's orders on appeal; it does not pass original orders of cancellation. The scenario mentions that SEBI is 'considering whether to cancel AWA's registration permanently,' and the legal position is that SEBI has this power under Section 12 after due inquiry. The right to appeal to SAT (not to a civil court) is a critical procedural safeguard.

questions.question: NSE's compliance officer has flagged 28 client accounts showing front-running patterns. If SEBI decides to pursue adjudication against AWA for this front-running in addition to the other violations, and the Adjudicating Officer is required to consider certain factors before imposing the penalty, which of the following factors is NOT among those the Adjudicating Officer is REQUIRED to consider under Section 15J of the SEBI Act?

options.A: The amount of disproportionate gain or unfair advantage, wherever quantifiable, made as a result of the default
options.B: The amount of loss caused to investors or any group of investors as a result of the default
options.C: The repetitive nature of the default, including whether the entity has been previously penalised by SEBI or any other regulatory authority for similar violations
options.D: The criminal antecedents of the directors and key managerial personnel of the entity, including pending FIRs and charge sheets filed by any law enforcement agency across jurisdictions

questions.explanation: Option D is NOT among the factors that the Adjudicating Officer is required to consider under Section 15J. Section 15J specifies three factors: (a) the amount of disproportionate gain or unfair advantage made, (b) the amount of loss caused to investors, and (c) the repetitive nature of the default. The 'criminal antecedents of directors including pending FIRs' is NOT a prescribed factor under Section 15J, though it sounds plausible. Options A, B, and C correspond to the three actual factors listed in Section 15J. Option C slightly paraphrases the 'repetitive nature of the default' to include 'previously penalised by SEBI or any other regulatory authority' — the core factor is the repetitive nature, which may include prior penalties. Option D is designed to trap students who assume that criminal background checks are part of every regulatory adjudication — while criminal antecedents might be relevant in a broader context (such as 'fit and proper' criteria for registration), they are NOT among the Section 15J factors for penalty quantification. The scenario's mention of multiple violations creates a realistic context for the repetitive nature factor.

scenarios.scenarioText: The Kapoor Group, a family-controlled business conglomerate, held 22.8% of the total voting rights in Meridian Steel Ltd. (MSL), a company listed on BSE and NSE with 3.2 crore outstanding shares trading at approximately Rs. 485 per share (market capitalisation approximately Rs. 1,552 crore). Mr. Dheeraj Kapoor, the patriarch and promoter, devised a plan to increase the family's control over MSL. Between January 15, 2026, and March 20, 2026, the following acquisitions were made through various entities: (i) Kapoor Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (KHPL), a Kapoor family investment company, purchased 85,000 shares on the open market (0.27%); (ii) Ms. Sneha Kapoor, Dheeraj's daughter and a non-executive director of MSL, purchased 42,000 shares (0.13%) in her personal demat account; (iii) Kapoor Family Trust acquired 1,10,000 shares (0.34%) through a block deal; and (iv) Pinnacle Ventures LLP, in which Dheeraj's son Karan Kapoor was a designated partner holding 60% interest, purchased 1,20,000 shares (0.375%). All acquisitions were funded through inter-corporate deposits from KHPL. After these acquisitions, the total holding of the 'promoter group' (as defined under SEBI regulations) reached 23.92% — crossing the 1% change threshold but not crossing 25%. None of the entities made any disclosure to the stock exchanges regarding these acquisitions. SEBI's surveillance division detected the pattern through bulk/block deal reporting discrepancies and issued a show-cause notice. Mr. Dheeraj Kapoor's counsel argued that: (a) the individual acquisitions by each entity were below 2% and hence not reportable, (b) Pinnacle Ventures LLP is not part of the 'promoter group' since Karan is merely a designated partner and not a controlling shareholder, and (c) even if the total crosses 1% change, the non-disclosure was inadvertent and should attract only a warning, not a penalty. Meanwhile, SEBI also discovered that Mr. Dheeraj Kapoor had simultaneously sold 50,000 shares of another listed company, Vertex Chemicals Ltd., based on advance knowledge of an impending CBI raid on Vertex's factory obtained from a senior government official at a private dinner on January 10, 2026. Mr. Kapoor's profit avoided (loss avoided by selling before the price crash) from the Vertex trades was Rs. 4.2 crore.

questions.question: Regarding the non-disclosure of the combined acquisition of 1.12% (from 22.8% to 23.92%) by the Kapoor promoter group in MSL shares, which penalty provision applies and what is the maximum penalty, considering that Mr. Kapoor avoided disclosure for the entire 65-day acquisition period?

options.A: Section 15A applies (failure to furnish information), with a maximum penalty of Rs. 1 crore (Rs. 1 lakh per day x 65 days = Rs. 65 lakh, which is below the Rs. 1 crore cap)
options.B: Section 15H applies (non-disclosure under takeover regulations), with a maximum penalty of Rs. 25 crore or three times the profit made/loss avoided, whichever is HIGHER
options.C: Section 15HB applies (other contraventions), with a maximum penalty of Rs. 1 crore, because non-disclosure under SAST regulations is a regulatory contravention not specifically covered by Section 15H
options.D: Section 15G applies (insider trading), with a maximum penalty of Rs. 25 crore or three times the profit, whichever is higher, because non-disclosure of acquisitions while in possession of information about one's own trading constitutes insider trading

questions.explanation: Option B is correct. Section 15H of the SEBI Act specifically deals with the penalty for non-disclosure of acquisition of shares and takeovers. When a person fails to make the disclosure required under the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, the penalty under Section 15H is not less than Rs. 10 lakh but may extend to Rs. 25 crore or three times the amount of profits made out of such failure, WHICHEVER IS HIGHER. This is the same 'higher of' formula as Section 15G (insider trading) and Section 15HA (fraudulent practices). Option A is the most tempting trap — Section 15A deals with failure to furnish information to SEBI, not failure to make disclosures under takeover regulations. While both involve 'non-disclosure,' they address different obligations: Section 15A is about responding to SEBI's information requests, while Section 15H is about the proactive disclosure obligation under SAST regulations. Option C wrongly categorises non-disclosure under SAST as a residual contravention under 15HB — Section 15H specifically covers this. Option D incorrectly labels non-disclosure as insider trading — these are distinct violations (non-disclosure under takeover code vs trading on UPSI). The scenario's 65-day period is a red herring for Section 15A computation — Section 15H does not have a per-day calculation.

questions.question: Mr. Dheeraj Kapoor sold Vertex Chemicals shares based on advance knowledge of a CBI raid, avoiding a loss of Rs. 4.2 crore. For this insider trading in Vertex shares, SEBI is considering BOTH adjudication (civil penalty) under Section 15G AND criminal prosecution under Section 24. Which of the following correctly describes the MAXIMUM exposure under BOTH provisions combined?

options.A: Civil penalty: Rs. 25 crore (being higher of Rs. 25 crore or 3 x Rs. 4.2 crore = Rs. 12.6 crore); Criminal prosecution: imprisonment up to 10 years OR fine up to Rs. 25 crore OR both — but SEBI must choose ONE track (civil or criminal) and cannot pursue both simultaneously
options.B: Civil penalty: Rs. 12.6 crore (3 x Rs. 4.2 crore, being the 3x profit/loss-avoided); Criminal prosecution: imprisonment up to 10 years OR fine up to Rs. 25 crore OR both — both tracks can be pursued simultaneously as they are independent proceedings
options.C: Civil penalty: Rs. 25 crore (being higher of Rs. 25 crore or 3 x Rs. 4.2 crore = Rs. 12.6 crore); Criminal prosecution: imprisonment up to 10 years OR fine up to Rs. 25 crore OR both — both tracks can be pursued simultaneously as civil adjudication is remedial while criminal prosecution is punitive
options.D: Civil penalty: Rs. 25 crore (being higher of Rs. 25 crore or 3 x Rs. 4.2 crore = Rs. 12.6 crore); Criminal prosecution: imprisonment up to 5 years OR fine up to Rs. 10 crore OR both — the reduced criminal penalty applies because the loss avoided is less than Rs. 5 crore

questions.explanation: Option C is correct on all counts. Civil penalty under Section 15G: the penalty is the higher of Rs. 25 crore or 3 times the profit/loss avoided. Here, 3 x Rs. 4.2 crore = Rs. 12.6 crore. Since Rs. 25 crore > Rs. 12.6 crore, the maximum civil penalty is Rs. 25 crore. Criminal prosecution under Section 24: imprisonment up to 10 years OR fine up to Rs. 25 crore OR both. Crucially, BOTH tracks can be pursued SIMULTANEOUSLY — civil adjudication (Section 15G) and criminal prosecution (Section 24) are independent proceedings. Civil adjudication is remedial/deterrent, while criminal prosecution is punitive. This is not double jeopardy because one is civil and the other is criminal. Option A correctly computes the civil penalty and criminal penalty but wrongly states SEBI must choose one track — this is the key trap. Option B correctly states both tracks can be pursued simultaneously but INCORRECTLY computes the civil penalty as Rs. 12.6 crore (applying only the 3x without comparing with Rs. 25 crore). Option D fabricates a reduced criminal penalty for lower amounts — Section 24 prescribes uniform penalties regardless of the amount of violation. The scenario's Rs. 4.2 crore figure is deliberately set below Rs. 8.33 crore (which would make 3x = Rs. 25 crore) to test the 'whichever is higher' computation.

questions.question: Mr. Kapoor's counsel argues that Pinnacle Ventures LLP (in which Karan Kapoor holds 60% as designated partner) is NOT part of the 'promoter group' and its acquisition of 1,20,000 shares should not be aggregated. If this argument is accepted and Pinnacle's acquisition is excluded, the remaining acquisitions total 0.74% (from 22.8% to 23.54%). Which of the following CORRECTLY analyses the disclosure obligation in that scenario?

options.A: No disclosure obligation arises because a change of 0.74% is below the 2% change threshold that triggers disclosure under the SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011, and individual entity-level acquisitions are each below 1%
options.B: Disclosure obligation still arises because under the SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011, any change in shareholding of the promoter/promoter group exceeding 0.5% must be disclosed to the stock exchanges within 2 trading days
options.C: No disclosure obligation arises for the promoter group aggregate, but each individual entity (KHPL, Ms. Sneha Kapoor, Kapoor Family Trust) must separately assess whether its individual acquisition triggers the disclosure threshold
options.D: Disclosure obligation may not arise under SAST for the change itself, but Ms. Sneha Kapoor, being a non-executive director of MSL, may have an independent disclosure obligation under SEBI (PIT) Regulations if her acquisition, combined with her directorial role, triggers the insider trading disclosure norms

questions.explanation: Option D is the BEST answer because it correctly identifies the nuanced position. If Pinnacle's acquisition is excluded, the aggregate change drops to 0.74%, which may fall below the SAST disclosure trigger for promoter group changes. However, the question tests whether students recognise that Ms. Sneha Kapoor, as a NON-EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR of MSL, has INDEPENDENT disclosure obligations under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015. Directors are 'designated persons' under PIT Regulations, and their trades require pre-clearance and disclosure regardless of SAST thresholds. Option A correctly notes that individual acquisitions are small but oversimplifies by citing a '2% change threshold' — the actual SAST disclosure thresholds are more nuanced (promoter group changes, crossing percentage thresholds, etc.). Option B fabricates a '0.5% change' threshold that does not exist in SAST regulations. Option C partially correct in separating individual assessments but misses the PIT regulation angle entirely. The scenario deliberately makes Ms. Sneha Kapoor a non-executive DIRECTOR — this dual role (promoter family member AND director) creates overlapping regulatory obligations that students must identify. The key scenario fact is her directorial position, which triggers PIT disclosure obligations independently of SAST.

questions.question: SEBI issued the show-cause notice and is proceeding with adjudication against the Kapoor Group. If Mr. Dheeraj Kapoor offers to settle BOTH matters (MSL non-disclosure and Vertex insider trading) through SEBI's consent mechanism, which of the following is CORRECT regarding the consent/settlement framework?

options.A: SEBI can settle both matters through consent orders provided Mr. Kapoor pays the settlement amount fixed by the High-Powered Advisory Committee, and once a consent order is passed, SEBI cannot subsequently initiate criminal prosecution for the same violations
options.B: Insider trading violations under Section 15G are specifically excluded from SEBI's consent mechanism and cannot be settled; only the non-disclosure violation under Section 15H can be considered for consent settlement
options.C: SEBI's consent mechanism allows settlement of adjudication proceedings, but it does NOT bar SEBI from initiating or continuing criminal prosecution under Section 24 for the same violations, since consent settles the civil/administrative proceeding only
options.D: Consent orders can only be passed at the SAT stage (during appeal), not at the SEBI adjudication stage; SEBI must first impose a penalty, after which Mr. Kapoor can offer settlement during the appeal before SAT

questions.explanation: Option C is correct. SEBI's consent and settlement mechanism (governed by the SEBI (Settlement Proceedings) Regulations) allows the settlement of civil/administrative proceedings, including adjudication proceedings under Chapter VIA of the SEBI Act. However, a consent order that settles the adjudication proceeding does NOT bar SEBI from initiating or continuing criminal prosecution under Section 24. This is because criminal prosecution is a separate track — the consent mechanism addresses the civil penalty, not the criminal liability. Option A is the most tempting trap — it correctly describes the consent process involving the Advisory Committee but wrongly states that consent bars subsequent criminal prosecution. Option B incorrectly claims that insider trading is categorically excluded from the consent mechanism — while certain serious violations may face higher settlement amounts or additional conditions, they are not entirely excluded from the framework. Option D fabricates a restriction that consent can only happen at the SAT stage — consent can be offered at any stage of the proceedings, including before SEBI itself. The key scenario facts are the TWO distinct violations (MSL non-disclosure + Vertex insider trading), testing whether students understand that consent for one does not affect the other, and civil consent does not preclude criminal prosecution.

questions.question: Regarding the Vertex Chemicals insider trading, Mr. Kapoor received the information about the CBI raid from a 'senior government official at a private dinner.' If SEBI wants to take action against this government official as a 'tipper' who communicated UPSI, which of the following CORRECTLY describes SEBI's jurisdiction?

options.A: SEBI has no jurisdiction over government officials; only the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) or the relevant government department can take action against the official for sharing confidential information
options.B: SEBI can issue directions under Section 11B against the government official for communicating UPSI in violation of SEBI (PIT) Regulations, and can also impose penalty under Section 15G on the official as a 'tipper,' since Section 11 and 11B do not limit SEBI's jurisdiction to market participants alone
options.C: SEBI can only recommend action against the government official to the Central Government under Section 11(2)(ia), but cannot directly issue directions or impose penalties since government officials are not 'intermediaries' or 'persons associated with the securities market'
options.D: SEBI can impose penalty under Section 15G on the government official only if the official also personally traded in Vertex shares; merely communicating UPSI without trading does not attract Section 15G penalty on the communicator

questions.explanation: Option B is correct. SEBI's jurisdiction under Section 11 and Section 11B is broad enough to cover any person whose actions affect the securities market, regardless of whether they are a market participant, registered intermediary, or government official. Under SEBI (PIT) Regulations, 2015, the prohibition on communication of UPSI (Regulation 3) applies to any person who is in possession of UPSI — there is no exemption for government officials. The 'tipper' (person who communicates UPSI) is independently liable under the PIT Regulations, and SEBI can impose penalty under Section 15G and issue directions under Section 11B. Option A wrongly limits jurisdiction to government disciplinary bodies — SEBI's securities market jurisdiction is independent. Option C creates an artificial limitation by restricting SEBI to 'recommending' action rather than directly acting — Section 11B does not contain such a restriction. Option D is a common misconception — Section 15G and the PIT Regulations penalise BOTH the person who communicates UPSI (tipper) AND the person who trades on it (tippee). The tipper need not personally trade to attract liability. The scenario fact that the information was obtained at a 'private dinner' does not create an exemption — the prohibition on communication of UPSI applies regardless of the setting.

scenarios.scenarioText: On February 1, 2026, SEBI passed a final order in the matter of Trident Capital Markets Ltd. (TCML), a SEBI-registered stockbroker, imposing a penalty of Rs. 18 crore under Section 15HA for market manipulation (synchronised trading and circular trading in 14 listed securities over a 9-month period from March to November 2025). The order was passed by Mr. Anand Rathi, the Adjudicating Officer (AO), who held the rank of Chief General Manager in SEBI. The order was served on TCML on February 3, 2026. TCML's board of directors decided to challenge the order. TCML's legal team filed an appeal before the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) on March 25, 2026 — 50 days after the order was served. TCML's counsel argued that the appeal should be admitted because: (i) the 5-day delay beyond the 45-day period was due to the company's board meeting being delayed by the non-availability of an independent director who was travelling abroad, and (ii) the delay is within the condonable period. Meanwhile, one of the 14 manipulated companies — Indus Polymers Ltd. (IPL), a listed company with 18,000 shareholders — filed an application seeking to be heard as an 'aggrieved party' in the SAT proceedings. IPL claimed it suffered reputational damage due to the price manipulation of its shares by TCML. SAT comprised a Presiding Officer (Justice Retired K.M. Sharma), a Judicial Member, and a Technical Member. During the hearing, TCML raised additional arguments: (a) the AO failed to consider the factors under Section 15J while quantifying the Rs. 18 crore penalty, specifically the loss caused to investors; (b) SEBI should have proceeded under Section 24 (criminal prosecution) instead of adjudication since the manipulation spanned 14 securities; and (c) the penalty of Rs. 18 crore is disproportionate since TCML's net worth is only Rs. 12 crore and the penalty would effectively shut down the firm. SAT reserved its order. After SAT delivered its judgment on June 15, 2026, upholding the Rs. 18 crore penalty but reducing it to Rs. 14 crore after re-evaluating the Section 15J factors, TCML decided to appeal further. TCML's counsel advised filing an appeal before the Supreme Court, but cautioned that the appeal ground was limited. SEBI, on its part, was also dissatisfied with the reduction from Rs. 18 crore to Rs. 14 crore and considered cross-appealing. The deadline for both appeals was approaching, with TCML's counsel noting that the limitation period for Supreme Court appeal was 60 days from SAT's order.

questions.question: TCML's appeal was filed on March 25, 2026 — 50 days after the order was served on February 3, 2026. Under Section 15T of the SEBI Act, which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates whether the appeal is within time?

options.A: The appeal is time-barred and cannot be admitted because Section 15T provides a strict 45-day period from the date of the order (not the date of service), and no condonation of delay is permitted under any circumstances
options.B: The appeal is within time because Section 15T provides a 60-day limitation period from the date of service of the order, and 50 days is within this period
options.C: The appeal is 5 days beyond the 45-day period from the date of the order, but SAT may condone the delay of 5 days if TCML shows sufficient cause, as Section 15T allows SAT to condone delay not exceeding a further 45 days
options.D: The appeal is within time because the 45-day period under Section 15T is computed from the date of receipt of the certified copy of the order, and since 'receipt' and 'service' may differ, TCML can argue it received the certified copy later than February 3

questions.explanation: Option C is correct. Under Section 15T of the SEBI Act, any person aggrieved by an order of the SEBI Board or the Adjudicating Officer may appeal to SAT within 45 days from the date on which the order is received. The proviso to Section 15T allows SAT to condone a delay not exceeding a further 45 days if it is satisfied that the person was prevented by sufficient cause from filing the appeal within the prescribed period. In this case, the order was served on February 3, and the appeal was filed on March 25 — a period of 50 days (5 days beyond the 45-day limit). Since 5 days is well within the further 45 days that SAT can condone, the appeal CAN be admitted if sufficient cause is shown. Option A is wrong — it denies condonation entirely, which contradicts the proviso to Section 15T. Option B fabricates a 60-day limitation period — the base period is 45 days, not 60. Option D attempts to create ambiguity between 'service' and 'receipt' — while the terminology is relevant, the scenario states the order was 'served' on a specific date, and that date is typically treated as the date of receipt. The scenario's mention of the board meeting delay due to an independent director's travel is a potential 'sufficient cause' argument, though SAT has discretion in evaluating this.

questions.question: TCML's counsel argued that SEBI should have pursued criminal prosecution under Section 24 instead of adjudication under Section 15HA, implying that the adjudication proceedings are invalid. Which of the following CORRECTLY addresses this argument?

options.A: The argument is valid — when manipulation spans more than 10 listed securities, SEBI is mandated to pursue criminal prosecution under Section 24 rather than civil adjudication, and the adjudication order is therefore void
options.B: The argument is valid because Section 24 and Section 15HA are mutually exclusive remedies; once an adjudication order is passed, SEBI loses the right to pursue criminal prosecution for the same violation, and vice versa
options.C: The argument is without merit because SEBI has the discretion to choose between civil adjudication under Chapter VIA and criminal prosecution under Section 24; there is no mandatory threshold that compels SEBI to choose one over the other based on the number of securities involved
options.D: The argument is partially valid — while SEBI can choose either track, once the penalty under Section 15HA exceeds Rs. 10 crore, SEBI is obligated to additionally initiate criminal proceedings under Section 24

questions.explanation: Option C is correct. SEBI has complete discretion to choose between civil adjudication (penalty proceedings under Chapter VIA, e.g., Sections 15G, 15H, 15HA, 15HB) and criminal prosecution (Section 24), or to pursue BOTH simultaneously. There is no provision in the SEBI Act that mandates criminal prosecution based on the number of securities involved, the quantum of manipulation, or the penalty amount. These are independent tracks — civil adjudication is conducted by an Adjudicating Officer, while criminal prosecution is filed before a court of competent jurisdiction. Option A fabricates a '10 securities' threshold that does not exist. Option B incorrectly treats the two remedies as mutually exclusive — they are concurrent, not exclusive. Option D invents a Rs. 10 crore threshold for mandatory criminal prosecution — no such threshold exists. TCML's argument is essentially asking SAT to invalidate the adjudication order because SEBI chose civil over criminal — this argument has no legal basis since SEBI's choice of enforcement tool is discretionary. The scenario mentions 14 securities as a red herring to make Option A seem plausible.

questions.question: SAT reduced the penalty from Rs. 18 crore to Rs. 14 crore after re-evaluating Section 15J factors. Both TCML and SEBI want to appeal to the Supreme Court. TCML's counsel stated that the limitation period for Supreme Court appeal is 60 days from SAT's order. Regarding appeals from SAT to the Supreme Court under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: The appeal to the Supreme Court lies within 60 days from the date of SAT's order, and the appeal can be on any ground — questions of fact, questions of law, or mixed questions of fact and law — since the Supreme Court exercises plenary appellate jurisdiction
options.B: The appeal to the Supreme Court lies within 60 days from the date of communication of SAT's order, but ONLY on a question of law arising from SAT's order; the Supreme Court cannot re-examine SAT's factual findings, including the re-evaluation of Section 15J factors
options.C: There is no direct appeal from SAT to the Supreme Court; TCML must first approach the relevant High Court under Article 226/227, and only then can it appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 136
options.D: The appeal to the Supreme Court lies within 90 days from SAT's order on any ground, and the 90-day period can be further extended by the Supreme Court under its inherent powers without any outer limit on condonation

questions.explanation: Option B is correct. Under Section 15Z of the SEBI Act, any person aggrieved by any decision or order of SAT may file an appeal to the Supreme Court within 60 days from the date of communication of the decision or order, but ONLY on a QUESTION OF LAW arising out of such order. This is a critical limitation — the Supreme Court cannot re-examine SAT's factual findings, including how SAT evaluated the Section 15J factors (disproportionate gain, loss to investors, repetitive nature). If TCML wants to challenge the Rs. 14 crore quantum, it must frame the challenge as a question of law (e.g., SAT applied wrong legal principles), not as a factual re-evaluation. Option A correctly states the 60-day period but wrongly includes questions of fact — this is the most tempting trap. Option C is factually wrong — Section 15Z provides a DIRECT statutory appeal from SAT to the Supreme Court, bypassing the High Court. This is different from the Companies Act structure (NCLT → NCLAT → SC). Option D fabricates a 90-day period and unlimited condonation. TCML's counsel's statement about '60 days' in the scenario is correct, but the counsel should have also cautioned that the ground is limited to questions of law only — the scenario hints at this by saying 'the appeal ground was limited.'

questions.question: Indus Polymers Ltd. (IPL) filed an application seeking to be heard as an 'aggrieved party' in the SAT proceedings, claiming reputational damage from the price manipulation of its shares. Which of the following CORRECTLY evaluates IPL's locus standi before SAT?

options.A: IPL has automatic locus standi because as a listed company whose shares were manipulated, it is directly 'aggrieved' by the AO's order, and SAT must hear IPL as a party respondent alongside SEBI
options.B: IPL has no locus standi because SAT proceedings are strictly between the person penalised (TCML) and SEBI; no third party, including an affected company, can intervene or be heard in SAT proceedings under any circumstances
options.C: IPL's locus standi depends on whether it can demonstrate that it is a 'person aggrieved' by the order within the meaning of Section 15T; since the AO's order was against TCML (not against IPL), IPL would need to show how the ORDER (not the underlying manipulation) adversely affects its rights or interests
options.D: IPL should file a separate complaint with SEBI under Section 11(2)(b) rather than intervening in SAT proceedings, because SAT's jurisdiction is limited to hearing appeals against SEBI's orders and does not extend to entertaining complaints about market manipulation

questions.explanation: Option C correctly identifies the key legal issue. Under Section 15T, the right to appeal to SAT belongs to 'any person aggrieved by an order' of SEBI or the Adjudicating Officer. The critical question is whether IPL qualifies as a 'person aggrieved' by the AO's ORDER. IPL is aggrieved by the MANIPULATION of its shares, but whether it is aggrieved by the PENALTY ORDER against TCML is a different question. IPL would need to demonstrate that the order adversely affects its rights — for example, if IPL wanted a higher penalty or additional directions. Option A oversimplifies — the fact that a company's shares were manipulated does not automatically make it a party to the penalty proceedings against the manipulator. Option B is too restrictive — SAT does have discretion to allow intervention by interested parties in appropriate cases, but it is not automatic. Option D correctly suggests that SEBI is the appropriate forum for complaints, but incorrectly limits SAT's jurisdiction — SAT can consider intervention applications. The scenario's detail about IPL's 18,000 shareholders and reputational damage is designed to evoke sympathy but does not change the legal analysis of locus standi.

questions.question: The Adjudicating Officer in this case, Mr. Anand Rathi, holds the rank of Chief General Manager in SEBI. TCML's counsel did NOT challenge his competence. Considering the requirements of Section 15I and comparing it with the scenario in Question 9 (where the AO held the rank of Deputy General Manager), which of the following statements about the Adjudicating Officer's appointment is CORRECT?

options.A: Mr. Anand Rathi, as Chief General Manager, is competent because the minimum rank required under Section 15I is Division Chief, and Chief General Manager ranks ABOVE Division Chief in SEBI's hierarchy; the DGM in Scenario 2 was incompetent because DGM ranks BELOW Division Chief
options.B: Both Mr. Anand Rathi (CGM) and Mr. V. Suresh (DGM from Scenario 2) are competent Adjudicating Officers because Section 15I merely requires the AO to be an officer 'not below the rank of a Whole Time Member,' and both CGM and DGM rank below WTM
options.C: Mr. Anand Rathi is competent because Section 15I requires only that the AO be appointed by SEBI, with no minimum rank requirement; the rank of the officer is relevant only for the quantum of penalty that can be imposed, with higher-ranked officers authorised to impose higher penalties
options.D: Both officers are competent because Section 15I requires the AO to be not below the rank of Deputy General Manager, and both DGM and CGM meet this requirement; the 'Division Chief' rank mentioned in the SEBI Act is an obsolete designation no longer in use

questions.explanation: Option A is correct. Under Section 15I, the Adjudicating Officer must be an officer of SEBI not below the rank of a Division Chief. In SEBI's organisational hierarchy, the typical order is: Assistant General Manager → Deputy General Manager → General Manager → Chief General Manager → Executive Director → Whole Time Member → Chairman. A Division Chief is typically at the General Manager or equivalent level. Therefore, a Chief General Manager (CGM) ranks ABOVE Division Chief and is competent, while a Deputy General Manager (DGM) ranks BELOW Division Chief and is NOT competent. This question reinforces the learning from Question 9 by providing the contrast — the same legal requirement applied to two different ranks produces opposite results. Option B raises the minimum rank to WTM, which is far too high — WTMs are not AOs but rather exercise independent direction-making powers. Option C denies any rank requirement, contradicting Section 15I's explicit text. Option D lowers the requirement to DGM and dismisses 'Division Chief' as obsolete — this is factually incorrect as Division Chief remains a valid designation. The scenario deliberately identifies Mr. Rathi's rank as CGM and states that counsel did NOT challenge competence — because at CGM rank, there is no valid challenge.
